Introduction

Starting a Child Care Facility in Oregon represents a meaningful opportunity to serve infants, toddlers, and preschool-aged children while building a compliant, sustainable care business. The need is immense; nearly all of Oregon’s 36 counties are considered infant and toddler care deserts, and only a fraction have an adequate supply of preschool slots. This gap between supply and demand creates a powerful incentive for entrepreneurs dedicated to early childhood development. Oversight and funding are administered by the Oregon Department of Early Learning and Care (DELC), with reimbursement and program funding coordinated through the DELC, including vital programs like Employment Related Day Care (ERDC).

With a clear state market signal of high, unmet demand and significant state investment, including over $189 million allocated for child care and pre-K in 2024, Oregon offers a supportive and high-potential market for providers. Reimbursement rates through the ERDC program range from $150 to $320 weekly per child, providing a stable revenue foundation. This environment creates a high-demand, underserved market for providers prepared to navigate the specific licensing, staffing, and compliance requirements set forth by the state.

This comprehensive guide walks you through every step of launching a Child Care Facility in Oregon, from understanding DELC regulations and licensing pathways to staffing your center, developing your budget, and preparing for inspections. Whether you are planning a small in-home program or a larger certified center, this framework will provide the clarity you need to succeed.

Table of Contents

  • Understand Oregon’s Child Care Facility Regulations
  • Choose the Type and Size of Your Program
  • Business Structure and Licensing
  • Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan
  • Secure a Suitable Facility or Office
  • Hire and Train Qualified Staff
  • Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans
  • Marketing and Referral Development
  • Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews
  • Frequently Asked Questions

Section 1: Understand Oregon’s Child Care Facility Regulations

Navigating the regulatory landscape is the first and most critical step in your journey. Oregon regulates Child Care Facilities through the Oregon Department of Early Learning and Care (DELC), which is responsible for the complete licensing, safety, and quality oversight for all certified and registered child care programs. The DELC’s rules are designed to ensure that every child in care is in a safe, healthy, and enriching environment. Providers serving Medicaid or federally funded populations must also comply with federal frameworks like the Child Care and Development Block Grant (CCDBG) requirements, Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), and HIPAA for any health information management.

The regulatory framework in Oregon emphasizes child safety, staff-to-child ratios, health and sanitation, and early learning curriculum standards. This means your facility, staff, and programming will be held to high standards. Key areas of focus include background checks for all staff, mandated reporter training for child abuse, safe sleep practices for infants, and detailed emergency preparedness plans. Licenses are not a one-time event; they typically require renewal every 1-2 years, contingent on maintaining compliance and passing periodic inspections.

Section 2: Choose the Type and Size of Your Program

After understanding the regulatory environment, your next step is to decide on the specific model of care you will provide. Oregon supports multiple program type variants, each with different licensing, staffing, and physical environment requirements. Choosing the right one depends on your goals, capital, and the specific community needs you aim to meet.

Oregon’s primary child care license types include:

  • Certified Family Child Care: This license is for a provider offering care in their own home for a small group of children. It’s an excellent entry point for entrepreneurs who want a smaller, more intimate setting. Capacity is typically limited to a specific number of children based on their ages.
  • Registered Family Child Care: This is also a home-based option but allows for a slightly larger group of children than a certified family program. It often requires an assistant and has more stringent space and safety requirements.
  • Certified Child Care Center: This license is for a program operating in a commercial facility. These centers can serve a much larger number of children, are organized by age groups (infant rooms, toddler rooms, preschool rooms), and have more complex staffing and administrative requirements.

Program size typically ranges from as few as 3-4 children in a home-based setting to over 100 in a large certified center. Demand is strongest across nearly all counties for infant and toddler care, which are considered care deserts. The 27 counties with inadequate preschool supply also represent high-demand regions. While competition may be lower in some rural areas, the most significant opportunity lies in addressing specific, high-demand niches. These include not only infant/toddler care but also outdoor/nature-based programs and culturally relevant care that reflects the diversity of Oregon’s communities.

Section 3: Business Structure and Licensing

With a program type selected, you must establish the legal and administrative foundation for your business. This involves formalizing your business entity and beginning the official licensing process. Providers in Oregon typically operate as an LLC, S-Corporation, or a Sole Proprietorship, especially for smaller, home-based programs. Consulting with a legal and financial advisor is crucial to select the structure that best protects your personal assets and optimizes your tax position.

Before you can apply for a license, you must complete several foundational steps:

  • Register your business name and entity with the Oregon Secretary of State.
  • Obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS, which is necessary for hiring employees and opening a business bank account.
  • Secure required insurance coverage, including general liability insurance and, if you have employees, workers’ compensation insurance.
  • Submit a complete licensing application to the Oregon Department of Early Learning and Care (DELC). This application is extensive and requires detailed information about your program, facility, staff qualifications, and operational policies.

Be prepared for a thorough process. Licensing timelines in Oregon generally range from 3 to 9 months, depending heavily on your readiness, the completeness of your application, and the time required for background checks and initial facility inspections. Starting early and being meticulously organized is key to a smooth approval process.

Section 4: Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan

A robust business plan is your roadmap to a sustainable and profitable child care facility. It should detail your financial projections, operational strategy, and market analysis. Understanding the costs and revenue potential is essential for securing funding and managing your business effectively.

Startup costs in Oregon can vary dramatically based on your program type. They typically range from $10,000 for a small, home-based program to $250,000+ for a fully equipped certified center. These costs include licensing fees, facility renovations or rent deposits, purchasing furniture and learning materials, insurance, and initial marketing. Operating expenses are driven primarily by staffing, which often represents 50-65% of total costs due to the strict staff-to-child ratios required for safety and quality.

Your revenue will come from a mix of private-pay families and state subsidies. A typical revenue snapshot includes:

  • ERDC Reimbursement: Ranges from $150-$320 weekly per child, providing a consistent income stream for qualifying families.
  • Private Pay Tuition: Rates vary by county and age group, with infant care commanding the highest rates. Research your local market to set competitive yet profitable tuition.
  • Grants and Special Funding: Keep an eye on state initiatives like the CHIPS Child Care Fund (HB 4098), which may offer grants for startup or expansion.

Providers who successfully manage enrollment and operate at or near 90-100% capacity can generally achieve healthy 15-25% profit margins. Your business plan should outline a clear path to reaching this target occupancy within your first 12-18 months to achieve break-even and long-term profitability.

Section 5: Secure a Suitable Facility or Office

Your physical location is more than just a building; it’s a core component of your program’s quality and compliance. Whether you are using a portion of your home or leasing a commercial space, it must meet the DELC’s stringent requirements. Location selection should consider local zoning laws, accessibility for parents, proximity to elementary schools or large employers, and the availability of a qualified workforce.

Facility requirements are detailed and non-negotiable. Key mandates include:

  • Sufficient Indoor and Outdoor Space: Oregon specifies a minimum amount of usable square footage per child, both indoors and in a secure, fenced outdoor play area.
  • Health and Safety Features: This includes child-proofed electrical outlets, secured storage for cleaning supplies and hazardous materials, smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, and first-aid kits.
  • Adequate Restroom Facilities: Age-appropriate toilets and sinks must be readily accessible to children.
  • Sanitary Food Preparation Area: If you provide meals or snacks, your kitchen or food prep area must meet health department standards.
  • Safe Environment: The facility must be free of hazards like lead paint, asbestos, and other environmental toxins. An initial inspection will verify compliance with all physical plant rules.

Section 6: Hire and Train Qualified Staff

Your staff is the heart of your child care program. Their expertise, compassion, and professionalism directly impact child development and parent satisfaction. Oregon’s regulations set clear minimum qualifications and training requirements for all personnel.

Required roles for a certified center typically include:

  • Center Director: Must meet specific educational and experience requirements to oversee all operations, staffing, and compliance.
  • Lead Teachers: Qualified individuals responsible for a specific classroom (e.g., infant, toddler, preschool), curriculum planning, and child assessments.
  • Assistant Teachers/Aides: Support Lead Teachers in classroom management, supervision, and daily activities.

For a family child care home, the primary provider must meet all training requirements, and any assistants must also be qualified and background-checked. All staff, regardless of role, must complete a series of mandatory trainings before working with children. Core training requirements include CPR/First Aid certification, Introduction to Child Care Health & Safety, Recognizing and Reporting Child Abuse and Neglect (Mandated Reporter), and Safe Sleep for infants. Additionally, Oregon requires ongoing continuing education hours each year to ensure staff remain current on best practices in early childhood education.

Section 7: Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans

Comprehensive, written policies and procedures are the backbone of a well-run, compliant child care facility. They provide clear guidance for staff, set expectations for parents, and demonstrate to the DELC that you have a plan for every contingency. These documents will be a primary focus of your initial licensing inspection.

Oregon requires written policies covering a wide range of operational areas. Your policy and procedure manual must include:

  • Health and Safety Plan: Detailed procedures for illness, sanitation, handwashing, and managing communicable diseases.
  • Emergency and Disaster Plan: Step-by-step instructions for fire, earthquake, lockdown, and other emergencies, including evacuation routes and reunification plans.
  • Staff Handbook: Outlines job descriptions, conduct expectations, training requirements, and disciplinary procedures.
  • Parent Handbook: Communicates your program’s philosophy, hours, tuition policies, and procedures for drop-off/pick-up.
  • Guidance and Discipline Policy: A clear, positive approach to managing child behavior that prohibits corporal punishment.
  • Medication Administration Policy: Strict protocols for storing and administering medication to children.

In addition to operational policies, you must show that you have a system for creating and maintaining individual care or service plans for each child. These plans must be developed in partnership with parents, reviewed regularly, and document the child’s developmental progress, needs, and goals.

Section 8: Marketing and Referral Development

With a severe shortage of child care in Oregon, your marketing focus should be less on broad consumer advertising and more on strategic relationship-building. Your primary goal is to become a trusted, known entity among the organizations that connect families with care.

Referrals for new child care facilities in Oregon typically come from:

  • Local Child Care Resource & Referral (CCR&R) Agencies: These state-funded agencies are the main hub for parents seeking care. Getting on their referral list is essential.
  • The State’s ERDC Subsidy Program List: Once licensed, being listed as a provider who accepts ERDC will drive referrals of qualifying families.
  • Local Employers: With new funding like the CHIPS Act, many large employers are seeking child care solutions for their workforce. Partnering with them can provide a steady stream of enrollments.
  • Community and Parenting Groups: Engage with local parenting groups on social media and in person to build a grassroots reputation.
  • Word-of-Mouth: The most powerful marketing tool. A reputation for high-quality, reliable, and compliant care will lead to strong parent recommendations.

Successful providers focus their energy on demonstrating compliance, being responsive to inquiries from referral agencies, and meticulously documenting positive outcomes for the children in their care. This professional approach builds the trust that fills your enrollment slots.

Section 9: Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews

Receiving your license is the beginning, not the end, of your compliance journey. Ongoing oversight is a standard part of operating a child care facility in Oregon. Oversight includes unannounced inspections from surveyors from the Oregon Department of Early Learning and Care (DELC). Local health and fire departments may also conduct their own periodic inspections.

DELC inspections are comprehensive, focusing on health, safety, and documentation. Surveyors will check staff files, child records, safety drills, and observe classroom interactions. Common deficiencies often cited during inspections include staff-to-child ratio violations, incomplete staff background checks or training records, safety hazards like uncovered outlets or accessible cleaning supplies, and improper record-keeping for attendance or medication. The best way to prepare for a survey is to maintain a state of constant readiness. This means conducting regular self-audits, keeping all documentation organized and up-to-date, and fostering a culture of compliance among your staff. Continuous quality improvement and audit-ready documentation are the keys to a clean inspection report.

Section 10: Frequently Asked Questions

Q: How long does it take to open a Child Care Facility in Oregon?

A: The process from starting your application to opening your doors typically takes 3 to 9 months. This timeline depends on the completeness of your licensing application, the time needed for background checks, and how quickly your facility can pass its initial health and safety inspections.

Q: What licenses are required to open a child care program in Oregon?

A: You will need a license from the Oregon Department of Early Learning and Care (DELC). The specific type depends on your program model. The main options are a Certified Family Child Care license (small, in-home), a Registered Family Child Care license (larger, in-home), or a Certified Child Care Center license (commercial location).

Q: What reimbursement is available for child care in Oregon?

A: Oregon offers significant financial support through the Employment Related Day Care (ERDC) program, which provides reimbursement ranging from $150 to $320 weekly per child for eligible families. Additionally, the state has allocated over $189 million for 2024, including funds from the CHIPS Child Care Fund, which may provide further grant or funding opportunities for providers.

Conclusion

Starting a Child Care Facility in Oregon is a challenging yet incredibly rewarding venture. The state’s significant need for quality care, combined with strong financial support through subsidies and grants, creates a fertile ground for new providers. Success requires careful planning, a deep understanding of the DELC’s regulatory requirements, and a steadfast commitment to operational discipline.

Providers who invest the time and resources to build a foundation of compliance, hire and train excellent staff, and cultivate strong relationships with referral agencies are positioned for long-term success and community impact. By following the steps outlined in this guide, you can move confidently from planning to licensure, ready to provide a vital service to Oregon’s children and families.
